The doorbell camera pings at 3:12 every night.

I work the overnight shift at the county hospital, so my telephone stays in my pocket with the volume turned all the way up. The notification arrives whether I am at work or at home, and it is never early or late. It is a bright electronic chime, like a spoon tapped against a glass. My coworkers teased me about the sound, because it was louder than any alarm on the ward. I tried to change the tone, but the settings menu offered only the one chime.

The first night, I was sitting in the staff room during my break, eating crackers from a vending machine. I opened the application expecting a delivery driver or a wandering cat, but I found a recording eleven seconds long instead.

A motionless figure stood on my porch in a dark gray hood, facing away from the entrance. The shoulders never moved, and the hands hung heavily at the sides. It looked heavy, as if it were holding something very carefully. There was no wind and no sound, and the figure never turned around, not even once. I watched it three times, and then I laughed, because laughing was easier than the alternative. My heart was beating hard enough that I could hear it over the hum of the vending machine.

Obviously somebody was playing a joke on me. I live alone in a small suburban house at the end of a quiet street, and I am the kind of person who waves at everybody. Perhaps a bored teenager had borrowed a sweatshirt, or perhaps the camera had a technical problem. I even wrote down the time of every recording in a small notebook, just to be sure. I deleted the recording and finished my crackers. Then I put the notebook away and told myself that was the end of it.

The next night the chime came again, and so did the figure, and by the fourth night I had stopped laughing completely. I started leaving the porch light on, and I started checking the street before I parked.

On the ninth morning I drove home at dawn, tired and cold, while the sun came up pink behind the rooftops. I parked in the driveway and walked toward my porch, where the boards were dry, because it had not rained for a week. Everything looked ordinary except for one small thing that I almost missed.

But across the boards there were footprints, wet and bare, shining in the early light. They crossed the whole porch and stopped at my front door. None of them led away.
